intro: How to join or start a debate club at school or in a homeschool co-op, the leagues and organizations, free places to practice and find topics, and classic speeches and debates worth studying.

p: If your school has a speech and debate team, ask the coach when practices meet; most teams welcome beginners at any point in the year. If it doesn't, you can start one (below). Homeschooled students can join a club in a homeschool league such as NCFCA or Stoa, or start one with other families. Adults can find public debate societies and clubs in many cities, and college students can join their school's team or start a parliamentary club.
The National Speech & Debate Association's starter guide suggests these steps:
ol: **Find an adult adviser.** Most tournaments require a school-approved adult to register students. The adviser doesn't need debate experience; a teacher, an alumnus, or (if the school allows) a parent or a local lawyer can act as sponsor.
**Get school approval.** Ask the main office or activities director how to form a club. Sometimes all you need is a signature to compete.
**Join a league.** Your adviser can sign the school up for NSDA membership (which has a fee) and for your state's league. That opens up resources, tournaments and student honors.
**Find tournaments.** Look on Tabroom.com for tournaments near you, ask the NSDA to connect you with your district, and start with a few local or online tournaments.
**Plan the money.** Tournaments charge entry fees, and travel costs money. Ask whether school or parent-group funds are available, and plan fundraising.

sections.h: Starting a club in a homeschool co-op
list: **Decide on a league, or none.** NCFCA and Stoa clubs follow their league's rules, resolutions and tournament calendar. An independent club can debate any topic, any format, any week.
**Recruit a parent coach** (no experience needed) and a few families with students about 12 and up. Younger students can do Oxford-style debates and short speeches.
**Meet weekly for 60 to 90 minutes.** A steady routine matters more than a perfect curriculum. Use the [Learn to Debate](/debate/learn/) chapters in order.
**Train parents as judges.** Every family can judge practice rounds with the printable [ballots](/debate/tools/ballots/) and a ten-minute talk on what judges look for.
**Hold a showcase.** An Oxford-style debate for families at the end of a term gives students a goal and an audience.

rows: Warm-up: a two-minute impromptu speech each, or the [fallacy spotter](/debate/tools/drills/)
Lesson: one Learn to Debate chapter, read aloud and discussed
Drill: four-step refutation or cross-ex practice in pairs
Practice round with the [timer](/debate/tools/timer/): one Public Forum or Lincoln-Douglas round, others flowing
Feedback: judges give one strength and one goal to each debater

sections.h: A first semester for a new club
ol: Weeks 1–2: [What a Debate Is](/debate/learn/what-is-a-debate/) and [Reading a Resolution](/debate/learn/resolutions/); dinner-table debates on beginner topics.
Weeks 3–4: [Building a Case](/debate/learn/building-a-case/); everyone writes one contention for each side of a beginner topic.
Weeks 5–6: [Refutation](/debate/learn/refutation-and-rebuttal/) and [Steelman vs Strawman](/debate/learn/steelman-vs-strawman/); rebuttal and steelman drills.
Weeks 7–8: [Cross-Examination](/debate/learn/cross-examination/) and [Flowing](/debate/learn/flowing/); first full practice rounds.
Weeks 9–10: [Weighing](/debate/learn/weighing/) and [Speaking Well](/debate/learn/speaking/); rounds with parent judges.
Weeks 11–12: a practice tournament or an Oxford-style showcase for families.

orgs.p: Most American high school debaters compete through a national association and their state's league; rules and topics can differ between them.

items.name: National Speech & Debate Association (NSDA)
items.about: The largest U.S. speech and debate organization and honor society. It publishes topics for Lincoln-Douglas, Public Forum and Congress, posts the NFHS policy topic, sets rules in its Unified Manual and runs a national tournament.

items.name: Your state's high school league
items.about: Many states run speech and debate through their activities association (for example, Texas's University Interscholastic League or the Oregon School Activities Association), with their own rules and state championships. Ask your school's activities office.

items.name: National Association for Urban Debate Leagues (NAUDL)
items.about: Based in Chicago; supports Urban Debate Leagues in about 19 cities at hundreds of middle and high schools, and holds a national championship.

orgs.p: Both leagues are volunteer-run Christian organizations for homeschooled students, with local clubs, regional tournaments and national championships.

items.name: NCFCA
items.about: Offers Team Policy and Lincoln-Douglas Value debate, ten speech events and moot court, in 14 regions with about 3,000 students (2022–23). Publishes its own resolutions and rules.

items.name: Stoa
items.about: Founded in 2009; offers Team Policy, Lincoln-Douglas and many speech events, and holds the National Invitational Tournament of Champions (NITOC).

items.name: USA Debate and the USA World Schools Debate Invitational
items.about: Run by the NSDA; selects the U.S. national team for the World Schools Debating Championships and runs a World Schools invitational.

items.name: World Schools Debating Championships
items.about: The annual international championship in the World Schools format.

items.name: National Debate Tournament and CEDA
items.about: College policy debate's two main organizations, with one shared topic each year.

items.name: National Parliamentary Debate Association (NPDA)
items.about: Nationwide parliamentary debate with a new motion each round and twenty minutes of preparation.

items.name: American Parliamentary Debate Association (APDA)
items.about: Student-run parliamentary circuit, mostly at colleges in the eastern U.S., where the government often writes its own case.

items.name: National Forensic Association
items.about: College individual events and a one-person policy-style Lincoln-Douglas debate.

items.name: American Mock Trial Association
items.about: Runs intercollegiate mock trial with one case for all schools; about 700 teams compete.

items.name: World Universities Debating Championship
items.about: The world championship in British Parliamentary debate; its Debating & Judging Manual is the format's main rulebook.

speeches.title: The Apology of Socrates
speeches.why: Socrates' defense at his trial, a model of answering accusations calmly and of arguing from principle.

speeches.title: Crito
speeches.why: Socrates argues with a friend about whether to escape prison; a careful back-and-forth that weighs obligations, useful for the [civil disobedience](/debate/topics/civil-disobedience/) topic.

speeches.title: Lives of Demosthenes and Cicero
speeches.why: How the ancient world's two most famous orators trained (Demosthenes practiced with pebbles in his mouth) and how their speeches shaped events.

speeches.title: Rhetoric
speeches.why: The founding book on persuasion: ethos, pathos and logos, the enthymeme, and the three kinds of speeches.

speeches.title: The Federalist, Nos. 1 and 2
speeches.why: Opening the case for the Constitution, Hamilton admits that "wise and good men" are on both sides of great questions, then argues his side hard: a lesson in fair-minded persuasion.

speeches.title: The Declaration of Independence
speeches.who: Thomas Jefferson and the Continental Congress
speeches.why: A classic argument in form: a principle, a long list of evidence, and a conclusion.

speeches.title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
speeches.why: A powerful argument for prudence and tradition against rapid change; read it alongside defenders of the Revolution to practice weighing.

speeches.title: Farewell Address
speeches.why: Advice to the nation on unity, parties and foreign alliances, often quoted in debates on foreign policy and term limits.

speeches.title: On Liberty
speeches.why: The classic case for free discussion, including the argument that you don't know your own side until you know the other side at its best.
speeches.note: Chapter II is on Project Gutenberg.

speeches.title: The Lincoln-Douglas debates
speeches.why: Seven debates on the spread of slavery, the format's namesake; study how each answered the other's strongest questions.

speeches.title: What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?
speeches.why: A masterpiece of turning an audience's own principles into an argument, with ethos, pathos and logos working together.

speeches.title: Gettysburg Address
speeches.why: Ten sentences that reframe a war around a principle; a lesson in brevity.

speeches.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
speeches.why: A point-by-point reply to critics that restates their objections fairly before answering them: steelmanning in action.

speeches.title: Hamilton's and Jefferson's opinions on the national bank
speeches.why: Two cabinet memos that are still the clearest statement of the broad and strict readings of the Constitution.
